candidato.titulo: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
candidato.resumo: The regulator says Tavneos was approved on the basis of manipulated study data. Should patients still have access to it?

texto_fonte:
In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies?
Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.”
At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects.
The advisory committee ultimately voted narrowly to recommend approval, and the FDA followed that advice, greenlighting the drug on October 7, 2021. The drug, marketed as Tavneos, started making its way into clinics. A year after approval, ChemoCentryx was acquired by Amgen, one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies. The cost, even today, isn’t minor: $220,000 per year, according to Drugs.com. In fiscal year 2025, sales of Tavneos reached nearly half a billion dollars.
This financial windfall has unfolded despite a long-roiling investor lawsuit—one that incidentally uncovered what the FDA today believes is evidence that ChemoCentryx employees manipulated the data in the pivotal trial submitted to the agency. In April of this year, the FDA issued a letter proposing that Tavneos be withdrawn from the US market, citing reports of serious, sometimes fatal, liver injury, and arguing that the drug now lacks “substantial evidence” that it works.

texto_fonte:
Different transcription systems shape chromatin behavior in distinct nuclear regions
Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which are further organized into chromatin. Chromatin has traditionally been divided into transcriptionally active euchromatin and relatively inactive heterochromatin. However, chromatin is not a fixed structure. Nucleosomes continuously move within the nucleus, and this motion is closely related to the physical organization and function of the genome.
Previous studies have shown that transcription can influence chromatin motion, but whether this effect is the same throughout the nucleus has remained unclear.
An international research team led by Kazuhiro Maeshima at the National Institute of Genetics and SOKENDAI has now investigated how different transcription systems affect the motion of distinct chromatin regions in living human cells. The work is published in the journal Cell Reports.
Tracking motion across chromatin classes
The researchers combined two technologies. The first was Repli-Histo labeling, a method previously developed by the group that distinguishes four chromatin classes, ranging from euchromatin (Classes IA and IB) to heterochromatin (Classes II and III). They further developed a machine-learning classifier to identify these chromatin classes objectively.
The second technique was single-nucleosome imaging, which allowed the team to directly track the movement of individual nucleosomes in living cells. This combination revealed that nucleosome motion becomes progressively more constrained from euchromatin toward heterochromatin. The researchers found that transcription does not constrain chromatin uniformly throughout the nucleus.
Different polymerases constrain different regions
When RNA polymerase II (Pol II), which transcribes most protein-coding genes, was inhibited using three different inhibitors, nucleosome motion increased in euchromatin (Classes IA and IB). Surprisingly, increased motion was also observed in heterochromatin around nucleoli. In contrast, heterochromatin at the nuclear periphery showed little change.
The team then examined RNA polymerase I (Pol I), which produces the major ribosomal RNAs inside nucleoli. Inhibition of Pol I produced a different response. Rather than broadly affecting chromatin, it selectively increased nucleosome motion in a late-replicating Class III heterochromatin population associated with nucleoli.
"Developing the machine-learning classifier allowed us to distinguish the four Repli-Histo chromatin classes objectively and reproducibly," says Ashwin of GITAM University. "These results show that transcription does not simply make chromatin more or less dynamic throughout the nucleus," says Maeshima. "Different transcription systems appear to impose physical constraints on different chromatin regions, depending on both their chromatin state and where they are located in the nucleus," says Minami.
Distinct constraints around nucleoli
The findings also highlight the special environment surrounding nucleoli. Both Pol II and Pol I transcription influence chromatin motion in this region, but they affect different chromatin classes. This suggests that nucleolus-associated chromatin is physically heterogeneous and is shaped by multiple transcription-dependent mechanisms.
The study provides a new way to examine how genome function is coupled to the physical behavior of chromatin in living cells. By combining Repli-Histo labeling, machine learning and single-nucleosome imaging, the approach can distinguish how different nuclear processes act on specific chromatin environments rather than treating the genome as a uniform polymer.
Publication details
Katsuhiko Minami et al., Machine learning-assisted Repli-Histo labeling reveals distinct transcription-dependent constraints on chromatin motion in living cells, Cell Reports (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118235

candidato.titulo: Spring News Roundup: First Release Candidates of Boot, Framework, Data, Security, Modulith, AI
candidato.resumo: There was a flurry of activity during the week of October 19th, 2026, highlighting: first release candidates of: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Data, Spring Cloud, Spring Security, Spring for GraphQL, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOS, Spring Modulith, Spring REST Docs, Spring AI, Spring Batch, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring LDAP and Spring Web Services. By Michael Redlich

texto_fonte:
There was a flurry of activity during the week of October 19th, 2026, highlighting: first release candidates of: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Data, Spring Cloud, Spring Security, Spring for GraphQL, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOS, Spring Modulith, Spring REST Docs, Spring AI, Spring Batch, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring LDAP and Spring Web Services.
Spring Boot
The first release candidate of Spring Boot 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a migration to the Ubuntu Resolute builder replacing the Noble Java Tiny Builder; and improved Uber-Jar performance using direct lookup of classes and resources in nested jars. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.
Spring Framework
The first release candidate of Spring Framework 7.1.0 ships with bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: improved nullability in the DataAccessUtils and LinkedCaseInsensitiveMap classes; and new overloaded methods, onRetrySuccess() and onRetryFailure(), defined in the RetryListener interface, that add an instance of the RetryState class in the parameter list such that listeners can access the retry state directly upon failure. Further details on this release, including removal of deprecated APIs, may be found in the release notes.
Spring Data
The first release candidate of Spring Data 2026.1.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades, RC1 upgrades to all of the subprojects and a notable new feature in Spring Data Redis that now forwards subscription notifications related to annotated listener methods if a bean implements the SubscriptionListener interface.
Spring Cloud
The first release candidate of Spring Cloud 2026.0.0, codenamed Paddington, delivers dependency upgrades, RC1 upgrades to all of the subprojects and a notable change where Spring Cloud Bus is no longer its own project and has been incorporated into Spring Cloud Stream. This release is based on Spring Boot 4.2.0-RC1. More details on this release may be found in this release notes.
Spring Security
The first release candidate of Spring Security 7.2.0 ships with bug fixes, dependency upgrades and two new features: an instance of the StrictServerWebExchangeFirewall class no longer detects a non-canonical-case HTTP method as a distinct value due to a change in the valueOf() method, defined in the Spring Framework HttpMethod class, that now normalizes casing; and RestClientOpaqueTokenIntrospector and SpringOpaqueTokenIntrospector classes now set the Content-Type header to application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and this what's new page.
Spring for GraphQL
The first release candidate of Spring for GraphQL 2.1.0 provides one bug fix that reinstates the Content-Length response header for WebFlux applications so that backwards compatibility is maintained and notable dependency upgrades such as: Spring Framework 7.1.0-RC1; Spring Data 2026.1.0-RC1; and Spring Security 7.2.0-RC1. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Session
The first release candidate of Spring Session 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: integrating the Spring Security Settings Plugin and Spring Security Maven Plugin; and standardizing the configuration of the public and private continuous integration environments. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Integration
The first release candidate of Spring Integration 7.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a deprecation of the default constructor in the SerializingHttpMessageConverter class to define a new constructor that contains the allowedPatterns attribute for improved security; and the ability to allow the DefaultJmsHeaderMapper class to set the outboundHeaderNames, inboundHeaderNames and excludedOutboundStandardRequestHeaderNames and excludedInboundStandardResponseHeaderNames to align with the DefaultHttpHeaderMapper class. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring HATEOAS
The first release candidate of Spring HATEOAS 3.2.0 provides notable dependency upgrades such as: Spring Framework 7.1.0-RC1; Spring Plugin 4.2.0-RC1; and Reactor 2026.0.0-RC1. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Modulith
The first release candidate of Spring Modulith 2.2.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new ABANDONED and RESUBMITTED enumerations, added to the EventPublication.Status interface, to distinguish between failed and abandoned event publications; and event publications are now completed, by default, using the Spring Framework TransactionSynchronization interface within a listener's transaction to avoid the possibility of a listener committing and the completion to fail. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring REST Docs
The first release candidate of Spring REST Docs 4.1.0 ships with one bug fix, a dependency upgrade to Spring Framework 7.1.0-RC1 and new features such as: improved nullability using JSpecify; and support for using the Spring Framework RestTestClient interface. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring AI
The first release candidate of Spring AI 2.1.0 provides dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new SessionService interface for creating and finding sessions that replaces the now-deprecated ChatMemory interface; and the ability for the OpenAiChatModel and DeepSeekChatModel classes to build an assistant message of each choice from ordered message parts. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Batch
The first release candidate of Spring Batch 6.1.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new @JobParameter annotation that injects a job parameter into a job or step scoped bean used to require a Spring Expression Language (SpEL) expression; and a new PageableItemReader class that serves as a type-safe alternative to RepositoryItemReader class to take a function from the Spring Data Pageable interface to a Slice interface. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring AMQP
The first release candidate of Spring AMQP 4.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: removal of the use of the noNullElements() method, defined in the Spring Framework Assert class, to allow the RabbitAdmin class and AmqpAdmin interface to accept null or empty arrays when declaring exchanges, queues, and bindings; and a simplification of the buildMessage() method, defined in both the AbstractAdaptableMessageListener and MessagingMessageListenerAdapter classes, to avoid unnecessary nesting when handling existing instances of the Message class and message conversion. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring for Apache Kafka
The first release candidate of Spring for Apache Kafka 4.2.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and one new feature that now writes out the value defined in the KafkaHeaders.DELIVERY_ATTEMPT header when using the CommonDelegatingErrorHandler class in conjunction with the deliveryAttemptHeader container property set to true. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring LDAP
The first release candidate of Spring LDAP 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: use of string parameterization in logging to avoid non-constant filename lengths; the addition of test cases for the DefaultObjectDirectoryMapperTests class; and string cleanup in the getStringAttribute() method, defined in DirContextAdapter class, to prevent a ClassCastException. More details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes and what's new page.
Spring Web Services
The first release candidate of Spring Web Services 5.1.0 ships with documentation improvements dependency upgrades and one new feature that allows an instance of the DefaultWsdl11Definition class to attach a policy document, such as a WS-Policy or WS-SecurityPolicy fragment, to every binding it generates. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.

candidato.titulo: Intel shifts production capacity from consumer to server CPUs in face of 'unprecedented' AI demand
candidato.resumo: Intel is expanding chipmaking and advanced packaging capacity across the U.S., Ireland, and Malaysia to meet surging AI-driven demand for data center CPUs amid shrinking PC market and persistent supply constraints.

texto_fonte:
Although the consumer PC market is shrinking and will continue to shrink in the coming quarters, Intel is confident that the overwhelming demand from the AI industry for everything that can compute or store data will offset declines in the client space. To that end, the company is reallocating some of its capacity from client to data center CPUs, expanding its Fab 24 in Ireland to make more Xeons, has begun equipment installation into Fab 62 in Arizona ahead of schedule and vows to make 18A chips there, and is expanding its advanced packaging capacity in New Mexico and Malaysia.
"The industry continues to navigate one of the most significant supply shortages in history, driven by the unprecedented demand for Super Intelligence," said Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, during the company's earnings call. "Against this backdrop, I am pleased by the progress we made growing our server supply in Q3. I am mindful about the ongoing challenges we face in the future quarters to keep pace with server demand."
More Intel 3-based Xeons
Intel's manufacturing expansion comes as demand for server processors continues to exceed supply despite substantial production increases over the next several quarters. The company's Data Center and AI (DCAI) business generated $7.3 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up 17% sequentially and nearly 80% year-over-year. Intel expects demand for data center CPUs to remain strong in 2027 – 2028 as AI infrastructure operators deploy more CPU-intensive agentic and inference workloads.
To meet demand for Xeon CPUs in the coming years, one of Intel's immediate priorities is to increase output of Xeon 6 'Granite Rapids' processors, which are made using its Intel 3 process technology. The company recently began expanding production capacity at its Fab 24 manufacturing complex near Leixlip, Ireland, but this capacity will only come online by the end of 2027, unless the move can be accelerated.
To further increase its Intel 3 capacity, Intel plans to convert some manufacturing resources at its Oregon facilities from Intel 18A to Intel 3. These resources were originally intended to manufacture Panther Lake client processors, but weaker PC demand has allowed Intel to prioritize higher-demand data center products. The company expects the additional Intel 3 capacity in Oregon to enter production in the second half of 2027.
"What we are taking offline to put Intel 3 into Oregon is 18A wafers, which we are generally going to build Panther Lake products," said Dave Zinsner, chief financial officer of Intel. "We see the opportunity with some of that capacity freed up to go produce more data center wafers."
Granite Rapids has already become Intel's fastest ramping server processor family, but demand continues to exceed available supply, according to the company's management. Intel is also improving manufacturing yields and reducing production cycle times to extract more usable processors from its existing capacity. According to the company, Intel 3 manufacturing costs have declined by approximately 15% since the first quarter of 2026.

Prepping for Diamond Rapids, Nova Lake
Intel is also accelerating the expansion of its leading-edge manufacturing operations in Arizona. The company is ramping Intel 18A production at Fab 52 and is accelerating equipment installation into the adjacent Fab 62, which is set to become the company's second high-volume manufacturing facility for 18A, 18A-P, and derivative process technologies.
These investments will support future Intel 18A/18A-P-based products, including server CPUs, although the company has not disclosed the precise allocation of manufacturing capacity between client and data center products at the facility. While the latter is natural, Intel said during the conference call that it expects to win some market share in the client space with its Core Ultra 400-series 'Nova Lake' CPUs, which will require the company to produce these parts in high volumes.
To support its capacity expansion, Intel aggressively procured new tools in the third quarter.
Not only wafers
While expanding production of Intel 3 and Intel 18A/18A-P wafers is a must to increase output of data center CPUs, producing more wafers will not necessarily solve Intel's supply problems. The company also faces shortages of advanced organic substrates required to package its multi-chiplet processors (or rather system-in-packages, or SiPs?) that rely on EMIB and/or Foveros 3D packaging technologies. Intel has been working with substrate suppliers to expand their production capacity and expects approximately 40% additional substrate capacity to become available in the second half of 2027.
"We are not only constrained on the wafer side, we are also constrained on the substrate side," Zinsner said. "So, it is important we get the substrate piece of this ramped up to be able to meet the demand."
In addition, Intel is expanding its advanced packaging operations in New Mexico and Malaysia to support growing demand from internal product groups and external customers. The company already uses its EMIB technology to connect multiple compute dies in Granite Rapids processors, while its newer Clearwater Forest Xeons combine EMIB with Foveros Direct 3D and hybrid bonding to stack Intel 18A compute dies on Intel 3 base dies. Additional packaging capacity will be essential as Intel increases production of these processors and introduces more complex multi-die products as well as assembles advanced system-in-packages using EMIB, EMIB-T, Foveros 3D, and other technologies for external clients.
"On Advanced Packaging, we are pleased by the progress we are making with EMIB and EMIB-T for our internal products," Tan said. "Both continue to see significant external customer traction as well. We continue to improve on execution, working with our supply chain to secure the capacity to meet the needs of our Advanced Packaging customers. We are also seeing robust progress in the readiness of Hybrid Bonding Interconnect (HBI), which is an enabler of 3D chip stacking for our upcoming server products."
Capital needed
Intel's expansions will require substantial capital. Intel expects its capital expenditure (CapEx) budget to reach approximately $20 billion in 2026 and increase significantly in 2027 (though it did not reveal any firm numbers). The company said firm purchase orders to semiconductor equipment suppliers increased by nearly 40% sequentially as it secured tools for its manufacturing expansion. Intel is also evaluating opportunities to accelerate construction of its semiconductor manufacturing complex in Ohio, where the first major structural truss was recently installed.
"We have made good progress securing the equipment required to support our growth plans with firm purchase orders to equipment suppliers increasing nearly 40% sequentially," Zinsner said. "We are also accelerating clean room build-outs, including Fab 62 in Arizona and exploring opportunities to accelerate in Ohio.
Yet Intel's capacity expansion will take time to produce results. New equipment must be installed and qualified, additional wafers must pass through lengthy manufacturing cycles, and substrate suppliers must increase their output (which will likely require them to procure new tools and install them) before Intel can ship more finished processors. Consequently, the company expects supply constraints to remain particularly severe during the first half of 2027, even as the client PC market is set to continue contracting.
Nevertheless, Intel expects its data center business to continue growing and believes that additional manufacturing capacity, higher yields, and improved substrate availability will enable it to capitalize on demand for AI infrastructure in the second half of 2027 and beyond.

candidato.titulo: The world mourns the passing of 'Star Trek's' Patrick Stewart with a galaxy of tearful tributes
candidato.resumo: "He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love."

texto_fonte:
As we all begin to absorb the bitter news of Patrick Stewart's death at the age of 86, a flood of personal tributes are pouring in, reflecting this global treasure's wonderful life lived with a dignity and bravado that few mortals possess.
We’re getting just a hint of what Patrick Stewart meant to those who worked with him or knew him throughout his stellar career. Whether on stage with the Royal Shakespeare Company, on TV as the dashing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and in Hollywood spectacles like 1984's "Dune," four "Star Trek" feature films, and the many "X-Men" movies in which he portrayed Professor Charles Xavier, Stewart was always the consummate professional. His final screen performance arrives on Dec. 18 with "Avengers: Doomsday" where he’ll present his Charles Xavier character once more.
"Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end," Ian McKellen wrote on Instagram of his "X-Men" co-star and friend. "You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love."
William Shatner, a fellow Enterprise captain, offered his profound sense of loss on Stewart's passing. The legends shared the screen in 1994's "Star Trek: Generations."
"What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor," Shatner posted on Facebook. "From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed."
Akiva Goldsman, co-creator of Paramount+'s "Star Trek: Picard" and "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds," delivered a sorrowful message in the aftermath of Stewart's death
"Patrick was not only a true lion of the profession, he was the rarest of alchemists, one who could literally turn the written word into flesh and blood," Goldsman wrote. "Patrick was kind, strong, fiercely intelligent, collaborative, vulnerable and wise. His Captain Jean-Luc Picard permanently expanded the universe of 'Star Trek' without measure. He will be deeply missed by this one fan and by so many more."
Stewart's "Star Trek: The Next Generation" family shared their grief and offered up poignant words to try to describe what effect he had on their lives and profession.

texto_fonte:
Julien Camirand Lemire, co-founder and CEO of Nord Quantique, is interviewed by Yuval Boger. Julien discusses Nord Quantique‘s bosonic code approach, which uses microwave photons in superconducting cavities to achieve quantum error correction without large qubit overhead, including their GKP and Tesseract code demonstrations and a quantum error correction gain that has more than doubled since 2024. They explore the company’s roadmap toward 10^-7 to 10^-9 error rates by 2032, the four-qubit system entering operation this year, and how Quebec’s Sherbrooke ecosystem has enabled a capital-efficient build. They also discuss high-rate codes, transmon-based scaling challenges, and much more.
Transcript
Yuval: Hello, Julien, thank you for being here.
Julien: Hi, Yuval, it’s a great pleasure to be here with you.
Yuval: So who are you and what do you do?
Julien: So I’m Julien Camirand Lemire, I’m co-founder and CEO of Nord Quantique. W e are a quantum computing hardware company building differentiated technology that really is anchored into error correction for scaling purposes.
Yuval: And you’re in Canada, right? That’s Canada with a Q, I believe.
Julien: Yes, Canada with a Q. We’re in Quebec, Canada, so it’s even more Q in the name. But yeah, we’re based in Sherbrooke, so we have offices here in the Sherbrooke ecosystem that is a pretty strong powerhouse in quantum in Canada, but also have offices in Montreal, which is well-known.
Yuval: So you got me interested in differentiated technology. Please explain.
Julien: Great. Yeah, I think, so we are a spin-off of this Sherbrooke ecosystem, as I’ve been mentioning. So we incorporated the company back in 2020. And at that time, I think it was pretty clear what we wanted to do, which is really build a technology. So a type of qubit that is capable of running quantum error correction. And the reason we were doing this is really looking at what the industry has been doing for the past 10 years. And I think we should just appreciate all the progress we have done as an industry in building quantum computing hardware that is more complex and scaling as well. So meaning that we have now as an industry systems that’s up somewhere between a hundred and thousands of qubits that are becoming more and more available. But despite this great progress, I think there are still some challenges, some very hard challenges that the industry is facing. And one of these challenges is errors as we are aware. So these qubits, they make errors, they’re prone to noise, and we need to deal with this. And the best way that the industry has started to also acknowledge is the need for quantum error correction. So this sort of error management layer that sits into the quantum computing stack that is there to detect and correct errors as they occur during a quantum computation. And the challenge with quantum error correction usually is the fact that it consumes a lot of resources. So you need some form of overhead inside your quantum computers to deal with these errors. So this overhead often comes in the forms of number of qubits. So you need a certain number of qubits more in your quantum computer to get there. And usually this factor is somewhere between 100 to 1,000. So that requires a larger and larger size system. But nothing tells you that this redundancy that is needed by quantum error correction has to come in the form of more qubits. And this is where we approach things a little bit differently at Nord Quantique. So the thing that you need for quantum error correction is a form of redundancy. And what we’re building is a technology that is called bosonic codes. These bosonic codes are made of microwave photons trapped into superconducting resonators. And the great thing about them is that you can trap multiple microwave photons inside a single cavity or single resonator, which provides you with the redundancy you need to do quantum error correction in a single cavity, which is really the embodiment of the hardware we’re building at Nord Quantique. So yeah, this is really what is differentiated about this technology is how we deal with quantum error correction, really trying to lower the overhead, sorry, to achieve quantum error correction in quantum hardware.
Yuval: There are other approaches, right? Amazon is developing a chip. Alice and Bob has a chip that they say will reduce the number of qubits required because I think it only, you know, it de-amplifies one type of error and you have to deal only with the other. How is that different than what you guys are doing?
Julien: Yeah, definitely. So bosonic codes is a large space. I think this just from the quantum perspective, so this is why we like these codes, but also just as the types of qubits we can build with bosonic codes, there’s many of them. Alluding to Alice and Bob who is developing certain types of cat qubit that is, as you’re mentioning, reducing one error channel. In our case, we use a different version that we call grid states. So the most notable example of these grid states is the GKP qubit. So we did some demonstration of that qubit early 2024. I think we’ve released our demonstration there. In these qubits, you can do full quantum error correction on a single of these qubits, so correcting for both X and Z errors, and this is what you will find in our 2024 paper. Beyond this also, these codes can be expanded to what we call multimode codes, so multiple, like in these cavity you can store multiple photons, you can also store photons of different frequencies, and these enables you to run different types of code, like the Tesseract code, which is a different example of the grid state that we have released in 2025.
Yuval: Do these cavities require cooling to near absolute zero, or do you operate at room temperature?
Julien: Yeah, thank you. Yeah, so we’re based on a superconducting platform, so what we use are the same building blocks as any superconducting qubit hardware, so we use resonators, of course. We use Josephson junctions to couple these resonators together and also to control them. So these operate at low temperature. But I think what is differentiated also from our architecture is that we need a smaller cryogenic environment to run systems in the end. So because we save resources for quantum error correction, there’s some layer of scaling that we don’t anticipate having to do. I mean, we’re reducing the overhead for quantum error correction by a large fraction with this cavity. And the purpose is really to build quantum computers, yes, in cryogenic environment, but in a constrained size. So something that will fit into 10 meters squared for more than 2000 of these logical qubits.
Yuval: So to get to real application, one doesn’t need a lot of qubits, just needs a large enough number of good enough qubits. And you’re basically saying that if I wanted a 200 qubit machine using your technology, I would need roughly 200 resonators, right? 200 cavities.
Julien: Yeah, that’s the purpose of the technology. So I think something that is interesting about that technology is you revert also to our paper in 2024. So we are able to do quantum error correction on single cavities. If you look at the performance of that system in 2024, it’s not where we need it to be in terms of real-world applications. So we still need to improve on quantum error correction and so on. The thing that is great about that system is we have a way to do this without increasing the footprint of the system. So this is the multimode code approach that I’ve mentioned. So building better codes in single cavities, for example, is one way to do this, but also we’re improving across the board. So as you’re mentioning, Yuval, so this is really the purpose of this system is really what we’d like to achieve, what we call the one-to-one ratio. So one cavity is an error-corrected qubit and scale the technology with this building block.
Yuval: If we just go into the 2024 paper, was it essentially quantum memory or were you showing quantum operations as in gates?
Julien: Yeah, so this paper in 2024 was a demonstration as a quantum memory. Since then, we have done gates that we presented at different conferences. And in our blog post, for example, in our blog page, you will see also the operation on gate of these qubits.
Yuval: Now you know what the next question is. So when can we see some gates?
Julien: What can we see in this? So we already have demonstrated gates. So you can see this on our webpage. I think the picture I have behind me is also a picture of our four qubit system. So this will be in operation this year and also something that we intend to work with partner to be operating with all these gates, but also working directly with error-corrected qubits. So this is for this year, the first release of that system and more publicly, if I would say.
Yuval: The 2024 demo also used some post-selection, right? Or was it just 100% error correction?
Julien: 100% error correction, yeah. So no post-selection. We also improved on that layer. So at that time, I think there’s one metric that we track internally is the quantum error correction gain. So by which factor are we improving sort of the performance of the hardware with quantum error correction? And now we also more than doubled on that number. So initially it was just barely making it. So I think we had a factor of 1.1 at that time. Now we’re beyond two and keep improving also the quantum error correction capabilities on these codes.
Yuval: Could you explain what that means? So let’s assume that you now, someone will test the four qubit system, maybe have some gates in it. You have built-in error correction. So what’s the gate fidelity? Is it a hundred percent or is it? Three nines, six nines, nine nines. I mean, what are we looking at?
Julien: Yeah, yeah, so we’re looking at, so depending on exactly what we’re looking into, so I think we’re talking around three nines is what we are working with right now in terms of operation on a single cavity and the two qubit, yeah, this is still improving. And also like we are adding the quantum error correction layer on top of all of this. What we think is interesting about this is the fact that we’re running quantum error correction today with these cavities. What it means is also we are improving this quantum error correction layer, but it comes with no surprise after this. I think this is how the system runs. You don’t have these things like post-selection. We’re not compromising on certain gates to allow for certain codes. So it’s the same codes that will be running on these systems. The other piece is also that we don’t have this classical layer that is usually there in quantum error correction to sort of do the syndrome measurement. So all the error correction that we’re running here is done autonomously, which is another differentiator of the quantum operation on that system.
Yuval: Three nines is nice, but certainly not enough. So does this approach take you to, what, a tera quop? How many nines does it take you to, or what do you have to do to get to the finish line?
Julien: Yeah, so I think it’s, so what we have to do is more of the same. So what I’ve mentioned earlier is, of course, the performance of the quantum hardware that we have today is not to reach usefulness. However, what we have unlocked with these cavities is also a way to improve performance with this multimode quantum error correction approach that I’ve mentioned earlier to unlock higher performance. And we have done demonstration of this. So you refer also to post-selection, which is something that we can do with the Tesseract code that enables us also to, which is sort of the two-mode version of the GKP code that I’ve mentioned earlier. And on that cavity, what we’ve shown is that we can operate with similar performance as the GKP code without post-selection, but when we turn that layer on, we’re able to shut an error channel off. And then all of a sudden, the logical performance, so the decay of the logical information, we were not able to measure it at that point, meaning that the decay was extremely low for that experiment. So what I’m saying here is that, yes, we need to improve, but we are improving by building these quantum error correction codes that are built on that artillery of multimode codes inside single cavities. So that’s the path forward for the company. Of course, we’re building bigger systems. That’s one axis of scaling. The other one is just pure quantum error correction improvement, which in each of the cavities that we’re building. And then what are we targeting? So we think we can reach 10 to the minus seven to 10 to the minus nine error rates, which in single cavity with these multiple techniques.
Yuval: When?
Julien: By when, exactly, that’s the right question. So our target for this is around 2032. So this is in terms of error rate, of course, we’re improving from now to then, unlocking these different codes with this.
Yuval: What you’re showing, what you showed in 2024, what you’re telling me now is very impressive. So I’m curious, why does it take six more years to get to what you’re describing? What’s the holdup? Is it you need just more money? Is there algorithmic issues that you have to solve? What is stopping you?
Julien: More money is always welcome, of course. But at the same time, I think this is something we should chat about also. We had a pretty capital efficient approach up to now. We believe also our technology allows for something that is more capital efficient growing from now on. I think some of the challenges that we have faced with bosonic codes also relates to the fact that it’s very different from the rest of the industry. I think a lot of the simulation tools we had to build, how we do quantum error correction for this hardware is also specific to that hardware. And this is part of the things that we have unlocked until now. And from now to the future, I think what we’re building is not only just better qubits, we’re also scaling the technology. So I’ve mentioned trying to achieve also these thousands of logical qubits that we’re aiming for these similar timeline that I’ve just mentioned is part of the journey that gets us there. So yeah, so more scaling, a lot of engineering and integration of this quantum error correction capability into scaled-up systems is what is ahead of us.
Yuval: There’s been a lot of press recently about high-rate codes. You know, Harvard released some results and others. So whereas previously one would imagine that you need a thousand physical qubits to get a good enough logical qubit, maybe the answer is we just need two, for instance. How are you thinking about these publications? Do they encourage you? Do they discourage you? What are your thoughts?
Julien: I think it, like, first of all, it’s impressive. It’s interesting. I think a couple of years back when people were looking at quantum error correction, I think it seems also impossible that we would have that discussion and reducing qubit count to these pairs. I think something that convinced us that the approach is the right one here. It’s also the trade-off between number of qubits and clock rate, we believe is good with the bosonic codes that we have right now. The other piece is also, we don’t need to rebuild the whole architecture for every new code that we’re implementing. As long as we have enough modes in our cavity, this is something that we can do on the fly as well. So no, it doesn’t scare us. I think it just shows progress. I think it shows also the importance of quantum error correction and the work that is needed to be done from an industry perspective.
Yuval: I believe you’ve transitioned from CTO to CEO, you know, a couple of years ago. What have you, how does that change your perspective? What have you done or what has the company done differently since that transition?
Julien: That’s a good, good question. So I think we expanded the leadership team also just to expand our bandwidth as a leadership team. Of course, I do more and more fundraising now, so this is just more of my work. But also, we’re building the company right now and we’re extending in that perspective. That switch of role was really just to enable us to be more scalable in that front. I think we have been successful to that point. So we’re really in a growth phase right now. So scaling the team, scaling the technology, but also just growing as an organization.
Yuval: Beyond fundraising, is there a commercial movement that you’re doing right now? Are you selling access? Are you selling computers? When you have that four qubit machine, how do you expect people to use it?
Julien: Yeah. So right now we are in discussions for a sale of a system. So that will be our first system sale. How we’re thinking about these system sales and just system access in general is we like to work with partners. So we have partners also that are developing applications on these. The machine also that we’re running with four or fewer qubits at the moment, and right now these partners have access also. Working also closely with what we call our application teams that support these external partners accessing the hardware or running any algorithms on these qubits as well. So this is how we also anticipate the next phases for commercial traction. At the same time, I think selling a ton of systems is not something that we will see from Nord. I think what you will see from us is selling more and more of these systems, but at the same time, our goal is really to have commercially viable quantum computers at the right moment. So we’re really aiming for usefulness here, and for us, this goes through unlocking quantum error correction and so on.
Yuval: You’re describing an architecture that is, well, maybe very complex to build, but potentially simple to use, right? And no need for a classical error correction there. Therefore, maybe the programming is rather simple. So what do you expect people to do with a four qubit system? I mean, obviously you can’t do something truly useful. The software sounds like it’s straightforward. What are you hoping to get from initial partners using that four qubit system?
Julien: I think, yeah, you’re right. So we won’t run any useful algorithms on those. Despite the fact that there’s some interesting angles sometimes, also there’s some specific things we can do with our present system that goes a little bit beyond this qubit world and quantum error correction. But I think the first piece is just running algorithms with quantum error correction on it, on top of it, and see how it impacts also the algorithms and so on. So it’s a good benchmark for people just to have access to an error-corrected system and us just to learn how these algorithms get to work with all the artillery in place.
Yuval: You mentioned capital efficiency. Is that by design or just it wasn’t the right time or was difficult to raise money some years ago?
Julien: No, no, no. It’s by design. So yeah, so I’ve mentioned, so we’re a spin-off of the Sherbrooke ecosystem. So there’s a quantum institute there, so it’s called Institut Quantique. So Quebec is a French-speaking nation, so everything is written in French as well. But Institut Quantique is one of the powerhouses also in quantum computing development across Canada, especially when it comes to hardware. So we’re really a spin-off of that environment. That environment also has a lot of history when it comes to microelectronics. So it is part of what we call the Northeastern Semiconductor Manufacturing Corridor that runs all the way down to Albany, ends up here in Sherbrooke and in Bromont, where fabs, but also with strong ties with the microelectronic industry, like plants like IBM packaging plants that is located in Bromont, Teledyne also has a plant there, they build the lens that are responsible for the rover that is on Mars right now. So there’s a lot of this sort of microelectronic industry, which means also that in our ecosystem, there’s a lot of tech transfer happening in this sort of sector. Quebec and Canada have invested a lot of money. In our case, it’s more than a billion of investment that we are leveraging from different pieces of infrastructure. Think of these fabrication facilities that we are using. So we have access to fabs that are also dedicated to superconducting fabrication. And it’s really our team operating this infrastructure on the ground that runs this. But we didn’t have to pay for this. Like, this was there, we’re just renting the access. And that is also true for some of the quantum hardware that we need to access, so fridges, a lot of the benchmarking facilities. So we could rent a lot of this equipment infrastructure. So this is money that we didn’t have to spend. So it really is by design. So the ecosystem in which we are is really embedded into this like tech transfer philosophy. And there’s a lot of infrastructure that was put in place that we were able to leverage. And now of course we’re growing. So that model where we rent a lot of the infrastructure has an end, but at the same time, it ends at the right time. I mean, we’ve done our demonstration and just from a capital perspective, so we’re getting money at the right time to do the right thing. And the second piece for us is really the technology. So the fact that we have this overhead reduction in terms of achieving quantum error correction and so on, means that we have smaller systems to build and this costs less in the end.
Yuval: As we get closer to the end of our discussion today, just a few quick questions. One is if the technology that you’re describing was not available, no bosonic codes, just gone, what modality would you prefer?
Julien: That’s a good question. It’s a tricky one. I think all modalities have sort of advantages and disadvantages. So beyond the bosonic codes, which I think has a really strong interest, especially as it comes to scaling technologies beyond this, we’re still a superconducting platform. The reason we are a superconducting platform is, of course, that’s a technology that was developed for a long time, so we know about it, but also it’s fast. I think that’s also something that we benefit from on the bosonics side. So the technology is fast. We keep that operation rate functioning for our bosonic qubits. And I think this will be important in the end. So I think that that’s a strong axis for superconducting qubits and so on. I do think this more standard transmon-based approach faces some challenges, especially when it comes to like connecting multiple fridges into a network environment. So there’s a lot of technology that needs to be advanced in order for the community to get there. But just if we are able to pass that wall in some sense, the fact that the technology is fast will remain a key advantage there.
Yuval: And as you think about the market evolution over the last couple of years, what has most surprised you?
Julien: I would say that the rate of evolution of the quantum error correction field, I think it’s, it’s impressive seeing, and it was a lot of the different demonstrations, whether it’s superconducting platform, neutral atoms, and now more and more people starting to bring that technology forward, to push for it. And we’re starting to, I think we will soon start to see the benefits of this in systems that will not only be playing with quantum error correction, but really start integrating that technology and scaling forward. Because like in our perspective, this is really one of the critical bricks that is in today’s most advanced systems and we really need to solve this as an industry if we want to have a useful system one day.
Yuval: And last hypothetical, if you could have dinner with one of the quantum greats, dead or alive, who would that be?
Julien: Sorry, say that again?
Yuval: If you could have dinner with one of the quantum greats, dead or alive, who would that be?
Julien: It’s funny because I was just at dinner with Michel Devoret, so Nobel Prize winner today actually, he’s visiting the ecosystem, so I’m pretty sort of on that end here. But, but all but that would have been my pick. Also, I think this Michel is not only somebody with whom we shared strong ties, but also he’s the founder of this demonstration of bosonic codes in superconducting circuits. So.
Yuval: Wonderful. Julien, thank you so much for joining me today.
Julien: Thank you so much, Yuval.
Yuval Boger is the Chief Commercial Officer of QuEra Computing.

- HP Googlebook 14: The HP Googlebook 14 is a stylish, lightweight laptop with a great screen, but its high price is hard to justify.
- Acer Googlebook 14: The Acer Googlebook 14 is a great premium laptop, but it’s not going to be everyone’s cup of tea. It’s only worth considering if you want a lightweight, high-end convertible laptop and you’re already deeply enmeshed in Google’s/Android’s ecosystem.
- Acer Chromebook Plus 514: The Acer Chromebook Plus 514 isn’t the most attractive ChromeOS machine, but it offers good performance and lots of storage for the price.
- Acer Chromebook Plus 516: The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 isn’t much to look at, but it benefits from an Intel Core i3 chip with solid performance and, at times, low sale pricing.
- Acer Chromebook Spin 315: Comfy to type on and handles the basics just fine, though the big bezels and limited charging options hold it back (hence why it’s not on the above list).
- Asus Chromebook Plus CX14: Performs better than models with Celeron CPUs.
How we test Chromebooks
The PCWorld team puts each and every laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Due to the cloud-based nature of Chromebooks, they go through a series of web-based tests. It wouldn’t be fair or possible to run the same kinds of tests on a Chromebook as we use on laptops because they exclusively run a completely different operating system.
For a more thorough explanation of our testing procedures, check out how PCWorld tests laptops.
Who curated this article?
Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo, and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen.
How to choose the best Chromebook
If you want something like a Windows or MacBook but cheaper, check out a Chromebook. Just keep in mind they’ve got some limits. They’re good for simple, everyday stuff but they don’t have a lot of RAM or storage, so they’re not equipped to handle more resource-intensive tasks like gaming or video editing.
We’ve got a guide that compares Chromebooks and Windows laptops if you want to figure out what’s best for you.
Key Chromebook features to consider
Operating system
Chromebooks only run Chrome OS, which is pretty easy to use. You can’t put Windows or macOS on them — you’re stuck with Google’s setup.
Processor
Shoot for a mid-range Chromebook if you can. They cost anywhere in the $400 to $600 range and many of them come equipped with Intel Pentium, Intel Core i3, or AMD Ryzen 3 processors. These Chromebooks run the browser smoother. They’re the best deal for the price. The fancier ones sometimes come with Intel Core i5 or AMD Ryzen 5 chips, which are way more powerful. Then there’s the new Kompanio Ultra chips, which are more powerful and AI-ready.
RAM
Lots of Chromebooks come with just 4GB of RAM, which isn’t much. Since they’re all about the web, you need enough RAM to keep your tabs from lagging. And with RAM prices being a bit more volatile lately, it’s worth opting for more if you can. If you can drop a bit more cash, you can grab a mid-range Chromebook with 8GB (or 16GB if you want to be extra safe), which runs way smoother.
FAQ
What is the best Chromebook?
PCWorld thinks the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 is the best all-around Chromebook. It’s got a solid Intel Core i5 processor, lots of ports, and handles everyday stuff really well. Basically, it’s a great pick if you want a reliable Chromebook without breaking the bank.
What is the best cheap Chromebook?
PCWorld’s pick for best budget Chromebook is the Asus Chromebook CX15. With a spacious 15.6-inch 1080p display and roomy keyboard, this Chromebook is comfortable to use and its Intel Celeron N4500 processor is able to handle daily tasks. If you’re after value, this Chromebook provides all the basics for less than $200.
What’s the difference between a Chromebook and a laptop?
A Chromebook’s just a laptop that runs Google’s Chrome OS instead of Windows or Mac. It’s mostly for web stuff like Google Drive and YouTube. Regular laptops are more powerful and can handle pretty much anything.
What is a Chromebook?
A Chromebook is a laptop that runs Google’s Chrome OS.

Scientists have uncovered an unexpected way certain metals can withstand extreme cold without becoming dangerously brittle. The discovery challenges long-standing ideas about how metals behave at extremely low temperatures and could help engineers develop tougher materials for some of the harshest environments imaginable.
The findings, published October 14 in Nature, reveal a previously unknown microscopic process that allows two experimental metal alloys to remain remarkably resistant to damage at just 20 kelvin, or -253°C (-424°F). The research was led by an international team from the University of California, Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the University of Oxford.
Why Extreme Cold Makes Some Metals Brittle
Cooling a metal generally increases its strength, but this improvement can come with a serious drawback. Certain metals become increasingly brittle as temperatures fall, making them more likely to crack or break instead of bending under pressure.
This problem is particularly important for a family of materials known as body-centered cubic metals (such as iron, tungsten, and chromium). Their atoms are arranged in a specific crystal pattern that can make them especially vulnerable to brittle failure in extreme cold. At temperatures approaching absolute zero, a small crack that might ordinarily be accommodated by the metal changing shape can instead spread and cause a fracture.
However, researchers discovered that two experimental alloys made from niobium and titanium behave very differently. Even when cooled to -253°C, both materials maintained an impressive ability to withstand damage. Neither showed a measurable shift toward brittle behavior at the lowest temperature tested.
The explanation lies in a surprising change in how the metals respond to stress. Rather than relying on their usual method of deformation, the alloys activate a different microscopic process that helps prevent cracks from spreading.
A Hidden Mechanism Helps Metals Resist Cracking
Under normal conditions, body-centered cubic metals bend and change shape through the movement of tiny defects within their crystal structures. These defects, called dislocations, allow layers of atoms to shift relative to one another, helping the material absorb stress without breaking.
As temperatures drop, however, these dislocations become increasingly difficult to move. With fewer ways to accommodate the forces concentrated around a crack, the metal becomes more likely to fracture.
The newly studied alloys have another way to respond.
Researchers observed a process called nanoscale 'twinning', in which tiny sections of the metal's crystal structure rearrange into mirror-image patterns. This occurs alongside a localized change in the crystal structure itself.
When these newly formed regions encounter the boundaries separating neighboring crystals, they produce concentrated areas of stress. Those stress concentrations generate additional defects, giving the metal new opportunities to deform rather than crack.
The researchers compare this behavior to a road system finding alternative routes when its usual roads become blocked by ice. As extreme cold makes conventional deformation increasingly difficult, the newly formed crystal structures provide other pathways for the metal to accommodate stress.
By creating these new pathways, the material can continue absorbing forces around potential fractures instead of failing abruptly.
A Breakthrough for Metals Used in Extreme Environments
The findings suggest a new approach to developing structural metals that can withstand exceptionally low temperatures. Such materials could be valuable in energy systems, transportation, and aerospace engineering, where components may encounter severe thermal conditions.
Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu (Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford) said: "For decades, the ductile-to-brittle transition has been viewed as a fundamental limitation of body-centered cubic metals. What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centered cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application."
The discovery also changes how scientists may need to think about what determines whether a metal becomes brittle. Previously, much of the emphasis was placed on how easily existing defects could travel through a material. The new results indicate that generating fresh defects may be just as important.
Lead author Dr. David Cook (University of California, Berkeley at the time of the study, now University of Cambridge) said: "Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal, but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures."
How Scientists Tested Metals at -253°C
To investigate how the alloys performed under such punishing conditions, the team conducted experiments using the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire.
The researchers used gaseous helium to cool metal samples to approximately -253°C. While directing a beam of neutrons through the materials, they used a specialized testing machine to stretch the samples by pulling from opposite ends.
This setup allowed the team to measure the forces the metals could withstand and determine how far they could stretch before breaking. The neutron measurements also helped researchers investigate what was happening inside the materials as they were deformed.
Afterward, the scientists examined the tested samples using powerful electron microscopes. These instruments revealed extremely small structural changes within the metal, including those near cracks that helped explain its unusual resistance to damage.
The team also used atom-probe analysis to determine how individual elements were distributed throughout the alloys. Combined with computer modeling, these measurements helped establish how the different microscopic processes worked together to prevent brittle failure.
The results offer more than an explanation for the surprising behavior of two experimental alloys. They identify a potentially useful strategy for designing metals that can remain tough even when conventional methods of deformation stop working, opening new possibilities for technologies that must operate in extreme cold.
The international collaboration included researchers from the University of California, Berkeley; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; the University of Oxford; the University of Bristol; the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, Science and Technology Facilities Council; the University of California, Irvine; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory; Texas A&M University; and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.

A corretora de criptomoedas Binance sofreu um ataque cibernético que resultou na perda de US$ 6,3 bilhões (ou R$ 34 bilhões, em conversão direta) em ativos financeiros na última quinta-feira (29). Especialistas atribuem a ação à Coreia do Norte e afirmam que este é o maior roubo da história do setor.
De acordo com a agência Reuters, toda a ação levou apenas 20 minutos. A investigação inicial apontou para uma vulnerabilidade no computador de um dos engenheiros que liberou acesso sem autorização para retirar o dinheiro, mas depois indicou que outros pontos de acesso foram comprometidos.
A Binance já atua em conjunto com autoridades nacionais e internacionais para investigar o caso e recuperar o prejuízo. Cerca de US$ 3 bilhões do valor perdido foram congelados, enquanto a empresa tenta retomar o montante restante.
Em comunicado oficial, a empresa afirma que usará os próprios fundos para cobrir as perdas.
O que acontece com quem tem ativos na Binance?
A empresa suspendeu os saques temporariamente por 48 horas como uma medida preventiva e garante que os ativos estão protegidos. Outros serviços da plataforma operam normalmente.
Em nota ao público brasileiro, a Binance diz que “os fundos de seus clientes permanecem seguros” e que segue requisitos de segregação do Banco Central do Brasil, nos quais criptomoedas são mantidas em cold wallets (carteiras frias, sem conexão com a internet) para ter uma camada de segurança extra.
